title: Optimize recommendations: batching & KV cache pricing review with Lucent Ware
summary: Redwood team walked Lucent Ware through Optimize recommendations for batching and prefix/KV cache with a cost model. Key themes: tradeoffs between latency and token cost, TTL strategy, sessionization, pilot scope, and security/enterprise requirements. Customer is evaluating Dedicated vs Hosted for data residency and compliance. Action items: send tailored pricing, security pack, and benchmark plan; schedule pilot kickoff next week.
action_items: Jamie Chen: Send Lucent-tailored cost model spreadsheet and shorthand pricing (due: 2028-10-05)
Ravi Patel: Draft benchmark plan for 1000 concurrent sessions including latency SLOs and sample prompt set (due: 2028-10-06)
Sofia Alvarez: Share Optimize runbook and recommended quantization profiles (due: 2028-10-07)
Markus Hale: Provide sample traffic histogram and retention requirements (due: 2028-10-04)
next_steps: Redwood to email pricing and security docs
Schedule 60-min pilot kickoff with SRE + SE
Run baseline throughput test in Redwood sandbox
Procurement to review contract terms and possible Dedicated PO
transcript_header:
Date: 2028-10-03
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Sofia Alvarez (Redwood Product), Markus Hale (Lucent CTO), Priya Iyer (Lucent ML), Diego Alvarez (Lucent SRE), Ava Chen (Lucent Procurement)
Recording: Yes
Location: Zoom
transcript_body: [00:00] Jamie Chen: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — we'll run through Optimize recommendations for your traffic, batching and prefix/KV cache recs, then cost model, then Q&A.
[00:18] Markus Hale: Sounds good. We're especially concerned about token unit economics — user-facing latency must stay under 600ms p95 for chat flows.
[00:27] Ravi Patel: Got it. We'll show a few simulated scenarios — low-latency priority vs cost-priority — and what the KV prefetch hit rates look like at different TTLs.
[00:43] Priya Iyer: Quick ask: our sessions are often short, like 2-3 turns average, but with occasional long-support threads. We currently use session-affinity on our side.
[00:55] Sofia Alvarez: That matters a lot for prefetch economics; short sessions reduce prefix reuse but sessionization + small TTLs can still help. We'll show the numbers.
[01:10] Diego Alvarez: Also want to confirm: we need to keep user data in eu-west-1 for compliance — leaning toward Dedicated or Private deployment.
[01:22] Jamie Chen: Understood. We'll call out Dedicated pricing and what Dedicated buys you: capacity isolation, region pinning, and audit logs with the Private option for on-prem later.
[01:35] (screen share starts) Ravi Patel: Ok sharing the Optimize console. This first chart is average batch size versus latency with continuous batching enabled.

[01:50] Ravi Patel: Notice as concurrency increases, batching improves tokens per second but p95 latency can climb if you allow larger batch windows. We recommend adaptive batch windowing with a 20ms cap for customer-facing chat.
[02:07] Priya Iyer: 20ms cap — is that on the request queue or on the GPU scheduling side?
[02:12] Ravi Patel: It's the batching window at the request router. It lets us batch while bounding tail latency. On our infra that maps to a 10-40ms scheduling variance depending on model size.
[02:31] Markus Hale: Are those numbers based on the Llama-like model you showed earlier? Our evaluation will use a 13B open model.
[02:39] Ravi Patel: Yes, simulated for a 13B variant quantized to 4-bit. If you run a heavier 70B family the window changes; we'll attach the sizing table in the spreadsheet.
[02:52] Jamie Chen: Switching to cache model — Prefix vs KV. Prefix caching stores common prompt prefixes, KV stores past KV cache entries for session warm starts.
[03:05] Sofia Alvarez: I want to highlight a mismatch we see — transcription sometimes labels product names weirdly, like "Redwood-Optimize" becoming "redwood optimist" — apologies in the auto notes.

[03:17] (laughter) Ava Chen: That's fine. Real question: how aggressive can we be with TTLs? Our privacy policy forces deletion after 30 days, but within that we can choose shorter TTLs to limit stale state.

[03:30] Ravi Patel: TTL selection is a cost/hit-rate tradeoff. For your traffic profile if you set KV TTL to 2 hours you hit ~65% of session restarts from KV, reducing token regen by about 35% in our model.
[03:46] Priya Iyer: 65% seems high for our app. That assumes session ids are sticky client-side, right? We sometimes shard sessions across devices.
[03:54] Ravi Patel: Correct — those sims assume session affinity. With cross-device you see fewer hits; introducing a lightweight session join key increases hit rate without full sticky routing.
[04:09] Markus Hale: Can you spell out the unit economics for that 35% token reduction?

[04:14] Ravi Patel: Sure — in the spreadsheet we run baseline tokens per session at 1,200 tokens. With 35% KV savings that's ~420 tokens saved per session. At hosted rates that's X cents; on Dedicated amortized it's a different delta — we'll show both.

[04:30] Jamie Chen: I'll call out practical numbers: Hosted per-token cost example in the sheet, Dedicated reserved capacity amortized cost per token under our conservative load — usually Dedicated beats hosted beyond ~8M tokens/month depending on model family.
[04:45] Diego Alvarez: When you say "beats", do you include the extra operational overhead? Our infra team does not want to manage GPU infra unless necessary.

[04:53] Jamie Chen: Dedicated includes managed infra from Redwood; you still have SRE involvement for networking and policies, but we handle serving runtime and autoscaling, so ops overhead is lower than self-hosting.
[05:06] Priya Iyer: Security checklist? SSO, RBAC, KMS, audit logs — we need SOC2 attestation and ability to review key rotation logs.
[05:15] Sofia Alvarez: We provide SOC2 Type II, SAML SSO, RBAC roles in the Console, and KMS integrations with both AWS KMS and customer HSM workflows. We'll share the security pack after this call.
[05:28] Ava Chen: Procurement note: we prefer PO-based contracts and a 60-day net. Any constraints on contract terms for Dedicated?
[05:36] Jamie Chen: Standard Dedicated is monthly or annual reserved; we can model a 12-month commit and show pricing. I'll flag finance to prep a redline-friendly term sheet.
[05:48] (10:00-minute mark) Ravi Patel: Back to caching. This chart shows miss-rate as a function of TTL. You can see sharp diminishing returns past 6 hours for your traffic shape.
[06:01] Markus Hale: Interesting. So a TTL of around 2-6 hours gets most of the benefit without long-lived storage of PII.
[06:08] Priya Iyer: What about cold-start cost? If a session misses KV, do we pay full token regen and then warm the cache immediately?

[06:15] Ravi Patel: Yes, misses pay full cost, but we recommend a lookahead prefetch for predictable long-running sessions — Redwood Optimize can prefetch KV on session start for a small upfront overhead which reduces tail regen.
[06:29] Diego Alvarez: Prefetching will increase egress or compute — how do we cap that?
[06:34] Ravi Patel: You can cap prefetch windows and only prefetch if session predictability crosses a threshold. Optimize gives recommendations per-route.
[06:43] Markus Hale: Can we see an example run where prefetch was used and how it affected 99th percentile latency?
[06:49] Ravi Patel: Yes — here's a slide from a prior customer: prefetch reduced p99 by ~200-300ms for complex multi-turn threads because it avoided full KV regens mid-session.
[07:02] Priya Iyer: Any risk to model quality with more quantization? We're using a fine-tuned 13B; quality hit is sensitive for us.

[07:09] Sofia Alvarez: We recommend model-specific quant profiles. For your tuned 13B, medium quant (4-bit) had <1% BLEU-ish drop on our internal evals for chat tasks, but we'll run a custom eval on your prompt set.
[07:23] Ava Chen: On pricing — can you share an illustrative table for hosted vs dedicated per token at the 1M, 5M, and 20M monthly buckets?
[07:31] Jamie Chen: Absolutely — included in the sheet. Quick take: Hosted is simpler but per-token is higher; Dedicated has lower marginal per-token once capacity commit is achieved.
[07:44] (timestamp jump) [10:15] Markus Hale: Walk me through the pilot. We want a 4-week pilot with metrics: p95 latency, tokens per session, cost delta, and failure rates.

[07:56] Jamie Chen: Pilot plan: Week 0: baseline data ingest and traffic capture. Week 1: sandbox runs with 10k sessions/day. Week 2: run prefetch + TTL variants. Week 3: full load test and cost review. We'll produce a final report.
[08:12] Priya Iyer: For the traffic capture, what do you need from us?

[08:16] Ravi Patel: A 7-day sample of session traces, request/response token counts, and a sample prompt set and user segmentation. Preferably CSV + small JSON metadata. Markus, that helps you are owner?
[08:27] Markus Hale: Yep I'll share. Expect histogram and a sample of user IDs. We'll anonymize PII.
[08:33] (lull) [20:00 mark] Sofia Alvarez: Quick demo of the Console recommendation card — it suggests batch window, cache TTL, and whether to prefetch. Here's how you apply suggestions to a route.
[08:48] Ravi Patel: Note the recommendation card also shows estimated monthly savings and a sensitivity band — we account for miss-rate variance.
[08:57] Priya Iyer: The sensitivity band looked large on one route. Is that because of sampling noise?
[09:02] Ravi Patel: Yes, smaller routes have higher variance. For low-volume routes we recommend conservative TTLs and to avoid aggressive prefetch until you have stronger telemetry.
[09:14] Diego Alvarez: About telemetry retention: How long does Redwood keep token-level traces? We may need 90-day retention for audits.
[09:21] Sofia Alvarez: Default retention is 30 days; enterprise packages can extend to 90/365 depending on plan. We'll put retention tiers in the security pack.
[09:33] Ava Chen: Are logs encrypted at rest by default?
[09:36] Sofia Alvarez: Yes, AES-256 at rest, and keys can be customer-managed via KMS.
[09:43] (small interruption) [30:00 mark] Markus Hale: We're curious about failure modes — if a node fails does Redwood fallback to a smaller model?

[09:52] Ravi Patel: We have routing policies that can fallback to a lower-cost model variant for availability. That includes deterministic fallback sequences and automatic retries with jitter to avoid spikes.
[09:59] Priya Iyer: Will fallback change semantics in chat? If we switch models mid-session the KV cache might be incompatible.
[10:06] Ravi Patel: Good point. We only fallback to compatible families with similar KV formats; if incompatible the system may drop cache and regen. We surface that in the Console and logs.
[10:18] Jamie Chen: Returning to pricing: I'll send you a model where you can tweak assumptions (miss rate, TTL, prefetch fraction) and see immediate delta on monthly cost.
[10:29] Markus Hale: Great. Can we add a column that shows estimated engineering time saved vs building our own cache router?
[10:35] Jamie Chen: Will do. We'll estimate eng effort savings conservatively — 4-6 engineer-weeks for a production-grade KV and routing + ops.
[10:46] (Crosstalk) Priya Iyer: Also want to confirm data residency for audit logs — will those stay in eu-west-1?
[10:52] Sofia Alvarez: For Dedicated in eu-west-1, yes. For Hosted we can pin region but logs may be replicated for reliability; we'll show options in the security doc.
[11:05] Ava Chen: Procurement question again — are there termination penalties on Dedicated reserved capacity?
[11:10] Jamie Chen: Standard reserved contracts have early-termination clauses; we'll list flexible options for pilots with monthly commitments.
[11:18] Markus Hale: Ok, final: what do you want from us this week to get the pilot started?
[11:22] Ravi Patel: Sample traffic + retention requirements + a pilot contact. Then we schedule the kickoff next Tuesday. We'll draft a short SOW.

[11:30] (wrap-up) Jamie Chen: Recap — Redwood to share: tailored cost model, security pack, pilot SOW, and benchmark plan. Lucent to share traffic sample and procurement contact. Next meeting: pilot kickoff — propose 2028-10-10.
[11:48] Markus Hale: 2028-10-10 works for us. Thanks team.
[11:53] Ava Chen: Thanks, bye.
[11:56] (call ends)
